title: Alarm And Warning Evaluation
summary: Alarm-and-warning evaluation examines whether alarms can be perceived, interpreted, prioritised, and acted on in the environment where a system is used. It is distinct from alarm lifecycle management and from the question of whether an alarm is technically present on screen.
keyFacts: The practice evaluates the full set of alerts, warnings, and alarm states in a system.
The evaluation is conducted against operating conditions rather than controlled viewing conditions.
Priority hierarchy, actionability, communication channels, false positives, nuisance alarms, mute behaviour, and operating-condition performance are core evaluation areas.
In regulated medical-device contexts, the evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8 and is part of the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process.
IEC 62366-1 governs the usability-engineering process for identifying and evaluating use-related risks; it does not specify what an alarm must look or sound like.
In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, 6 comparable surgical devices were evaluated under operating theatre conditions.
In the Kardion MCS Controller engagement, the submitted design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required.
In the Cox Marine cluster displays engagement, scenario testing produced a requirement for a two-level alarm architecture.
In the Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX engagement, the evaluation produced a requirement for two distinct alert levels for routine and critical notifications.
In the Gexcon CFD simulation engagement, the evaluation produced requirements for a three-point warning architecture.

bodySections.heading: Alarm And Warning Evaluation in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies alarm and warning evaluation as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: What Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation Assesses
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation is the practice of examining a system's alerts, warnings, and alarm states against operational criteria that determine whether users can perceive, interpret, prioritise, and act on them under real use conditions.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation assesses operational function, not only technical presence. An alarm can be visible and accurately triggered while still failing operationally if it does not communicate the required action, cannot be distinguished from lower-priority alerts, or depends on a communication channel that is unreliable in the operating environment.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation is separate from alarm lifecycle management, alarm rationalisation, priority assignment, and the standards that codify those activities. This practice evaluates how alarms behave for users once they exist in a system.

bodySections.heading: Operational Criteria for Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation assesses the full alert set against the criteria that determine whether each alarm can be perceived, interpreted, prioritised, and acted on in time. The evaluation asks whether the alarm communicates both the problem and the next step.

The evaluation is conducted against operating conditions rather than controlled viewing conditions. The relevant questions are whether an alarm can be perceived in the real environment, whether it can be interpreted quickly enough to act on it, whether it directs attention to the right place, and whether it communicates the necessary action.

In Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, alarm-and-warning evaluation is used as diagnostic evidence before redesign work and as formative evidence when alarm designs are being developed in regulated medical-device contexts.

bodySections.heading: Priority Hierarchy in Active Alarm States
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation checks whether the system has a defined alarm priority structure and whether that structure is visually expressed. A user looking at an active alarm state should be able to determine whether the condition requires immediate intervention or whether it is informational.

When multiple alarms are active simultaneously, alarm-and-warning evaluation examines whether the highest-priority condition receives the most prominent treatment. A system can fail this test even when every alarm is technically visible.

bodySections.heading: Actionability of Warnings and Alarms
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation distinguishes between alarms that close the action loop and alarms that open it. An actionable alarm communicates the condition and the next step. A non-actionable alarm communicates only that something is wrong.

In time-pressured environments, an alarm that reports a condition without specifying the next action can create delay, interpretation burden, or incorrect response.

bodySections.heading: Communication Channels Used by Each Alarm
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation examines the channels each alarm uses, including colour, sound, icon, position, text, and vibration. The evaluation identifies where an alarm depends on a single channel that may fail under operating conditions.

Colour-only indicators are unreliable in variable lighting. Sound-only alarms can be inaudible in noisy environments. Text can become unreadable when vibration affects the interaction. Alarm-and-warning evaluation identifies where these single-channel dependencies remove the signal when the operating context changes.

bodySections.heading: False Positives, Nuisance Alarms, and Mute Behaviour
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation estimates how frequently alarms trigger under conditions that do not require action. Nuisance alarms are treated as a driver of alert fatigue because repeated non-actionable alerts can train habitual dismissal.

The evaluation identifies which alarm types are most likely to create dismissal behaviour and whether that behaviour could extend to genuine alerts.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation also reviews what happens when a user silences an alarm. The evaluation distinguishes between muting that produces silence while preserving visual presence and muting that makes an active alarm invisible. An alarm that disappears entirely when muted creates a pathway to a state where an active alarm exists but is no longer visible to the user.

bodySections.heading: Operating-Condition Testing for Alarm Behaviour
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation tests significant alarms under the conditions of actual use. Relevant conditions include lighting, noise, attentional load, and the physical position from which users interact with the device.

In embedded systems, alarm-and-warning evaluation must be conducted in the real operating environment or approximated to that environment closely enough to expose the same perception and interpretation risks. This is adjacent to usability testing under realistic constraint and edge-case and degraded-mode analysis when warning, fault, or degraded states affect the user's ability to act.

bodySections.heading: Regulatory Alignment in Medical-Device Contexts
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In regulated medical-device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8, the collateral standard for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment. The evaluation covers priority tiering requirements, the prohibition on colour as the sole differentiating attribute between priority levels, mute behaviour requirements, and alarm state visibility requirements.

IEC 62366-1 governs the usability-engineering process through which the use-related risks behind those alarm requirements are identified and evaluated. IEC 62366-1 does not specify what an alarm must look or sound like.

Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

bodySections.heading: When Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation Is Used
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation is used during Sandbox Experiments when an existing system is being reviewed. In that context, the evaluation contributes to the diagnostic evidence base established before design work begins.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation is also used as part of complex product audits. Alarm architecture failures are described as a recurring finding in audits of high-consequence systems, and the evaluation provides structured evidence for specific recommendations.

In regulated medical-device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation runs throughout Iterative System Building as part of the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process. Proposed alarm designs are assessed against IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements before they are finalised.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation typically follows state-and-transition review, which identifies system states including alarm states. It precedes the redesign work covered by warning-and-alarm clarity improvement.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation produces structured findings about alarm behaviour under operating conditions. Outputs can include findings on priority hierarchy, actionability, communication-channel dependency, nuisance alarm exposure, mute behaviour, operating-condition performance, and standards alignment.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation can also produce alarm architecture requirements. In documented engagements, outputs included requirements for redundant non-colour cues, two-level alarm architecture, distinct alert levels, and staged warning architecture.

In regulated medical-device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation can produce documented design requirements traceable to identified use-related hazards. The Kardion MCS Controller evidence describes requirements for the alarm layer that were tied to identified hazards rather than framed as general design recommendations.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and Limits of Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation does not replace the broader alarm-management discipline. Alarm lifecycle, rationalisation, priority assignment, and the standards that codify those activities are separate from this evaluation activity.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation does not treat technical visibility as sufficient evidence that an alarm works. The practice evaluates whether the alarm can be perceived, interpreted, prioritised, and acted on under operating conditions.

The engagement evidence is context-specific. The documented examples include surgical devices, a cardiac support controller, marine cluster displays, a consumer building-control interface, and an expert simulation tool. Findings from one context should not be generalised to all alarm systems without further evaluation.

In regulated contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation aligns with IEC 62366-1 use-related hazard identification for alarm conditions. It also aligns with IEC 62682 and ISA-18.2 alarm management standards where applicable.

strongClaims: Alarm-and-warning evaluation examines alerts, warnings, and alarm states against operational criteria, not only against whether they appear on screen.
The practice evaluates priority hierarchy, actionability, communication channels, nuisance alarms, mute behaviour, operating-condition performance, and regulatory alignment where applicable.
In regulated medical-device contexts, the evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8 and runs as part of the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process.

In the Kardion MCS Controller engagement, the alarm evaluation produced alarm architecture requirements tied to identified use-related hazards, and the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted with no design changes required.
weakerClaims: In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, 6 comparable surgical devices were evaluated and colour-only communication was identified as the primary failure mode across the competitive set.

In the Cox Marine cluster displays engagement, scenario testing identified that tile-level fault visibility did not direct attention to the priority engine and produced a two-level alarm architecture requirement.
In the Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX engagement, the evaluation produced a requirement for routine and critical notification levels for a non-technical audience across 54 countries.
In the Gexcon CFD simulation engagement, the evaluation produced requirements for setup-stage warnings, pre-run contradictory-input warnings, and post-detection error specification.
limitations: Alarm-and-warning evaluation is distinct from alarm lifecycle management, alarm rationalisation, and priority assignment.
The practice evaluates operating-condition performance rather than controlled viewing-condition performance.
The engagement evidence is context-specific and should not be generalised to all alarm systems without evaluation in the relevant operating environment.
IEC 62366-1 is described as governing the usability-engineering process; it does not specify what an alarm must look or sound like.
Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.
